name: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques
text:
# Interpolation and Sampling Techniques

Also called: Trilinear Interpolation (DRR), Trilinear rendering

## Overview
Interpolation and Sampling Techniques constitute the family of methods responsible for retrieving scalar values from discrete voxel grids at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays, thereby reconstructing a continuous scalar field to mitigate discretization artifacts such as aliasing and blockiness [S1, unofficial][S2]. This family solves the fundamental problem of spatial reconstruction in [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md), distinguishing itself from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel itself rather than the statistical distribution of sample points, and from [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) by operating in [voxel space](#3074-voxel-space.md) rather than depth space.

## Shared principles
All interpolation schemes in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in voxel space to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$ V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i $$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2].

## Subtopics

### [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md)
[Interpolation schemes for volume rendering](#817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md) reconstruct a continuous scalar field from discrete voxel data to evaluate density or opacity at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays. This family solves the problem of discretization artifacts (aliasing, blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling while balancing computational cost against spatial smoothness. It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel itself rather than the statistical distribution of sample points, and from [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) by operating in voxel space rather than depth space.

### [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md)
[Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](#1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) reduces jagged edges and aliasing artifacts in volume rendering by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the results. It sets itself apart from standard single-ray casting by explicitly addressing the coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling, which causes abrupt intensity changes along object silhouettes. Compared to [Supersampling](3493-supersampling.md), which generally implies a [uniform grid](#920-uniform-grid.md) increase in resolution, this method employs specific deterministic offset patterns to distribute samples efficiently within the pixel footprint.

### [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md)
[Depth to Distance Conversion](#2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) transforms sampled depth values ($z_{vals}$) along a ray into segment lengths ($dists$) required for volume rendering integration. It accounts for the viewing angle by scaling the depth differences with the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction. This method is distinct from [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md) as it focuses on metric length calculation rather than value estimation, and from [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) as it operates on already sampled points [G].

### [Alpha Grid Mask](2430-alpha-grid-mask.md)
The [Alpha Grid Mask](#2430-alpha-grid-mask.md) is a module that stores a 3D alpha volume and provides efficient sampling of alpha values at arbitrary 3D coordinates using PyTorch's `grid_sample` function, enabling [ray filtering](#2681-ray-filtering.md) based on opacity. It serves as the core sampling primitive for volume rendering to incorporate spatially varying opacity constraints derived from external supervision or geometry masks. It differs from direct intensity sampling by applying a linear remapping to the sampled values to ensure they fall within a valid $[min\_opacity, max\_opacity]$ interval, preventing complete occlusion or invisibility artifacts.

### [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md)
[Sampling and Jittering](#2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) is a [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that casts rays from the camera through a 3D voxel grid, samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding artifacts, and composites the result using front-to-back [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md). It distinguishes itself from [uniform ray sampling](#1261-uniform-ray-sampling.md) by perturbing sample positions to break up [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md) patterns, and from stochastic methods by using a deterministic, pre-computed jitter texture rather than runtime random number generation.

### [Supersampling](3493-supersampling.md)
[Supersampling](#3493-supersampling.md) is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results, effectively sampling the scene at a higher spatial frequency than the displayed resolution. It addresses the coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling, which causes visible artifacts such as jagged edges (staircase artifacts) and moiré patterns, particularly along object silhouettes where intensity changes abruptly. Unlike standard single-sampling, supersampling provides a more accurate color representation for each pixel by integrating the signal over the pixel area.

### [Epipolar Sampling](3899-epipolar-sampling.md)
[Epipolar sampling](#3899-epipolar-sampling.md) is a technique for aggregating features from multiple views by sampling along epipolar lines rather than along camera rays in 3D space. It solves the problem of efficiently correlating information between a reference view and target views without performing full 3D volume rendering or explicit 3D reconstruction during the encoding phase. Unlike [standard volume rendering](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md) which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent parameter prediction.

### [Space Warping (Log+Warp)](5815-space-warping-log-warp.md)
[Space Warping (Log+Warp)](#5815-space-warping-log-warp.md) is a [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) strategy for [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) that warps 3D space towards the view cell center using radial distortion. It solves the problem of high-frequency background details requiring excessive network capacity by dampening these frequencies while preserving foreground detail. It sets itself apart from standard [logarithmic sampling](#5814-non-linear-logarithmic-sampling.md) by applying an additional inverse-square-root warp to the encoded coordinates, ensuring that sample locations in space remain consistent across different viewpoints.

### [Gradient-Based Interpolation by Sample Splatting](9072-gradient-based-interpolation-by-sample-splatting.md)
A real-time interpolation algorithm that reconstructs source radiance $L_x$ throughout a volume from a small set of samples, using both radiance values and radiance gradients to achieve higher accuracy than standard interpolation.

### [MLS Volume Reconstruction](9796-mls-volume-reconstruction.md)
A volume rendering technique that reconstructs a smooth scalar field from discrete samples using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation, allowing for adaptive preintegration to handle the computational cost of the scalar field evaluation.

### Slab-based Ray Sampling
[Slab-based Ray Sampling](#2853-slab-based-ray-sampling.md) is a variant of [pre-integrated volume rendering](#5327-pre-integrated-volume-rendering.md) that processes the volume in slabs of thickness $2d$ defined by three successive samples (front $s_f$, middle $s_m$, back $s_b$) [S2]. The next slab is indexed by $(s_f, s_m, s_b)$ with the correlation $s_f = s_b$, ensuring continuity between adjacent slabs [S2]. After retrieving the scalar values for $s_f, s_m, s_b$ from the 3D volume, the color and opacity values are determined by a 3D texture fetch in a [3D pre-integration table](#2854-pre-integration-lookup.md), which is then composited using a front-to-back algorithm [S2].

### Space-covering volume sampling
Space-covering [volume sampling](#7111-volume-sampling.md) is a technique proposed by Kraus to extend pre-integrated volume rendering to multidimensional transfer functions [S3]. It addresses the limitation of standard pre-integration, which typically handles only scalar transfer functions, by using a space-covering approach to approximate the integral over multidimensional feature spaces [S3].

## Background
Trilinear interpolation, often referred to as Trilinear rendering, is a widely used technique in volume rendering, particularly for generating Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR) [S1, unofficial]. It offers a significant speed advantage over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method [S1, unofficial]. For instance, rendering a standard AP view with Siddon's method takes approximately 25 ms, whereas trilinear interpolation with 25 sample points takes only 737 μs [S1, unofficial]. The rendering cost of trilinear interpolation matches that of Siddon's method only when the number of sample points ($n\_points$) is increased to approximately 2,000 points (25 ms) [S1, unofficial]. The performance scales linearly with $n\_points$, taking 1.03 ms for 50 points, 1.65 ms for 100 points, and 66 ms for 5,000 points [S1, unofficial].

The concept of slab-based sampling is rooted in pre-integrated volume rendering, where pre-computed tables are used to account for the integration of optical properties along ray segments [S2]. Space-covering volume sampling was introduced to handle multidimensional transfer functions, building upon earlier work that used second-order functions to improve the accuracy of pre-integrated TF integrals [S3].
